messages:
Alex Park: Quick heads-up — ran the trace-harness against prod traces (sample slice A) with the new kernel selector + async batching heuristics and saw a mismatch in token streams when KV-cache warmup is enabled. outputs diverge ~30 tokens in on avg, not just whitespace. :thinking:
Maya Singh: Ugh. Is this deterministic across reruns of the same trace set?
Alex Park: No — rerun the same trace + seed produces different logits after warmup, but if I disable KV warmup it becomes stable.
Samir Patel: Can you paste the exact command and the kernel selection log? curious if the selector flips to the fused-attn path mid-request.
Alex Park: Sure — ran: `./harness/playback --trace-dir s3://prod-traces/A --seed 42 --kv-warmup yes --kernel-policy auto --batch-mode async`
Alex Park: Kernel log snippet:
```
2026-11-07T14:02:01Z kernel: selected=fused_attn_v2 device=rtx4090
2026-11-07T14:02:01Z kernel: switching-path from=naive_attn to=fused_attn_v2 reason=seq_len>128
```
Maya Singh: Hmm switching path mid-request could change accumulation order and cause fp sum nondeterminism. But that alone shouldn't change discrete token choices that early. Are we sure tokenization/anonymization didn't alter prefix lengths?
Alex Park: I double-checked. Anonymizer replaced identifiers but preserved token boundaries. Also ran with raw traces (no anon) and still saw divergence, so not an anonymization artifact.
Samir Patel: Any profiling data? batch sizes, kv-hit ratios, latency windows?
Alex Park: Profile (slice avg): batch_size histogram [1: 62%, 2: 25%, 4+: 13%], kv_hit_ratio ~ 0.42 during warmup, cpu->gpu memcpy spikes correlate with divergence windows.
Maya Singh: That low kv_hit ratio during warmup is suspicious. If KV cache warmup warms partial prefixes, maybe we have inconsistent KV merge ordering across async batches.
Samir Patel: Possible race: when async batching groups inflight requests, KV writes might be replayed in different order vs original. That would explain nondeterministic cache state and downstream outputs.
Alex Park: Good call. I added a deterministic barrier after warmup in the harness and reran — now outputs are stable. So harness-level ordering matters. But production runtime uses the same async heuristics; we need trunk fix.
Maya Singh: For an apples-to-apples comparison we should: 1) run two harnesses with identical ordering semantics (deterministic barrier vs none), 2) capture kernel selection traces + per-token RNG seed, 3) run parity checks that ignore tokens before a configured stable point (e.g., after 64 tokens).
Alex Park: Implemented per-token RNG logging and a parity check that tolerates early instability. With that parity we can surface real regressions. Current diff looks like kernel-selection-induced nondet, not a model-weight regression.
Samir Patel: Next steps: open a PR to a) add an explicit KV-merge-order test in replay-harness, b) add a kernel-selector guard to avoid mid-request path flips, c) run a 24h sweep on slice B.
Alex Park: Filing issues now and kicking off the sweep. Job posted: <https://ci.internal/runs/73321|harness-sweep-73321> :rocket:
replay-bot: Job 73321 queued — estimated run time 9h.
Maya Singh: Nice. Also let's add a short note to eng-runtime playbook about how anonymization must preserve token boundaries — saw one earlier that collapsed emojis into single tokens and confused parity checks.
Samir Patel: Agreed. I'll draft the playbook blurb.
Alex Park: Thanks all. I'll attach a small repro (trace slice + minimal harness flags) to the issue. :thumbsup:
